questions.q: In the C4 model, what question does the Context level answer?
options: What is this system, and who or what people and other systems talk to it?
Which individual classes and functions implement the system?
Which internal modules make up one deployable piece?
Which specific AWS instance types are used in production?
questions.explain: Context is the whole system drawn as a single box, showing the people and other systems around it -- the level a non-technical stakeholder would be shown.

questions.q: According to this lesson, at which C4 level should most enterprise architecture documentation and cross-team diagrams actually live?
options: Code level
Component level
Container level
There is no recommended level; it varies randomly by team
questions.explain: Container level shows the major deployable pieces and how they communicate -- detailed enough to be useful, abstract enough to stay stable, which is why most architecture docs should live there.

questions.q: What does a dashed rectangle represent in the trust-boundary notation described in this lesson?
options: A deprecated resource scheduled for deletion
A zone where everything inside shares the same level of trust, such as a VNet, account, or subnet behind a firewall
A component that has not yet been deployed
The physical boundary of a cloud provider's data center
questions.explain: A trust boundary is drawn as a dashed rectangle around a zone sharing one level of trust; data-flow arrows crossing out of it are the points worth a reviewer's attention.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an unlabeled data-flow line is a problem?
options: It makes the SVG file size too large to render
It is forbidden by the Azure Architecture Icons license
It cannot be converted into Terraform code automatically
It tells a reviewer nothing about whether a boundary crossing is encrypted, authenticated, or even expected
questions.explain: A data-flow arrow should be labeled with what's moving and how (e.g. HTTPS, gRPC, JDBC) and point in the real request direction -- an unlabeled line just shows two things are connected, without saying anything useful about the crossing.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend using exactly one official icon set per diagram, matched to one abstraction level?
options: Mixing icon sets or abstraction levels is purely a matter of visual preference with no real downside
Only one icon set is legally licensed for commercial use
A diagram that mixes official icons with ad-hoc boxes, or mixes zoom levels, forces the reader to guess whether the inconsistency means something or is just noise
Diagramming tools technically cannot render more than one icon set at a time
questions.explain: Inconsistent icon sets or abstraction levels on one diagram make a reader unsure whether a visual difference is meaningful, which breaks the diagram's usefulness as the team grows past people who already know the context.
